findings.issue_text: Denial cache is consulted before the fresher permission cache and DB; stale negative entries can override just-granted permissions, and permDenialCache is not invalidated on permission/role changes, so revocations→grants can be denied for up to the full cache TTL

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates unbounded, user-influenced fields with '_' separators, allowing key collisions (e.g., name 'a_b'/parent 'c' vs name 'a'/parent 'b_c') causing one resource's denial to deny a different resource; should use delimiter-safe or hashed encoding
When cached permissions exist but s.checkPermission returns an error, the function returns the error instead of falling back to the DB, so a corrupt cache entry can hard-fail authorization

Denial entries use checkReq.ParentFolder in the key but lookup keys are built before normalization/validation; if ParentFolder is optional/empty while Folder is set, semantically different requests may hit or miss the denial cache inconsistently or cache the same resource under different keys

permissionCacheUsage with "false" is incremented unconditionally after a cached-permissions miss, including when getCachedIdentityPermissions failed for a non-user identity type, skewing metrics; the err is silently discarded

getCachedIdentityPermissions returns cache.ErrNotFound for TypeRenderService on every request, forcing a full DB fetch every time; this regresses caching for render-service identity types (or the new switch is misleading dead code)

The cached permission map (map[string]bool) is returned by reference from the shared cache and used across concurrent requests; if any consumer mutates it, the cache is corrupted for all readers—it should be treated as immutable or copied
On denial-cache hit, requestCount is incremented with "false", "true" labels identical to the DB path, making cache-hit denies indistinguishable from DB denies in metrics
No test covers invalidation of permDenialCache when permissions change (e.g., a previously-denied resource must be allowed after a write/batch-set that clears permCache)

The removed test 'should return permissions from cache if available' is only partially replaced; no test asserts that getUserPermissions still populates the cache after a DB fetch, so a regression where the cache is never written would go unnoticed

When cached permissions are used for List, results may be stale with no versioning; List on a cache hit never validates against the DB even when permCache was populated long ago relative to idCache (different TTLs), which can list stale resources

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache is consulted before the fresher permission cache and DB; stale negative entries can override just-granted permissions, and permDenialCache is not invalidated on permission/role changes, so revocations→grants can be denied for up to the full cache TTL

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check(), the new permDenialCache is consulted first (permDenialCache.Get(...) then immediate return Allowed:false) before checking the permission cache (getCachedIdentityPermissions) or the DB (getIdentityPermissions). A denial entry is written on any DB deny (if !allowed { permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }) and is never cleared on subsequent allows (neither cache-allow nor DB-allow paths delete it). Therefore, if permissions/roles change from deny→allow within the shortCacheTTL window, the stale negative entry will continue to force denial until expiry, overriding both updated permCache and the DB result.

This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both the golden and candidate comments flag the same core issue: cache keys are built by concatenating components with '_' which can produce ambiguous keys and collisions when components contain underscores (or otherwise overlap), leading to incorrect denial cache hits and permission errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: When cached permissions exist but s.checkPermission returns an error, the function returns the error instead of falling back to the DB, so a corrupt cache entry can hard-fail authorization

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeds, it immediately calls `s.checkPermission(ctx, cachedPerms, checkReq)`. If that returns an error, the code logs and returns `return deny, err` without attempting `s.getIdentityPermissions(...)` from the DB (the DB path is only reached when cache lookup fails or when `allowed` is false). This creates a new hard-fail path where a bad/corrupt cached permission map can cause authorization to error out rather than falling back to the DB.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial entries use checkReq.ParentFolder in the key but lookup keys are built before normalization/validation; if ParentFolder is optional/empty while Folder is set, semantically different requests may hit or miss the denial cache inconsistently or cache the same resource under different keys

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the denial cache key is built from `checkReq.ParentFolder` (`permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)`), but there is no shown “normalization/validation” step that happens after the key is constructed, nor evidence that `ParentFolder` could be empty while `req.Folder` is set. The mapping from the incoming `authzv1.CheckRequest` fields (which include `Folder`) to `checkReq.ParentFolder` is not visible in this diff, so the claimed inconsistency cannot be verified from the provided changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permissionCacheUsage with "false" is incremented unconditionally after a cached-permissions miss, including when getCachedIdentityPermissions failed for a non-user identity type, skewing metrics; the err is silently discarded

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, `permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()` is executed after the cache attempt regardless of why the cache path didn’t return an allow (i.e., both when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns an error and when it returns perms that don’t allow). `getCachedIdentityPermissions` can return `cache.ErrNotFound` for identities where caching isn’t applicable (e.g., `types.TypeRenderService` always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`) or even a non-NotFound error (e.g., `unsupported identity type`), and `Check` discards `err` (only acts on `err == nil`). This will skew the “false” metric in those cases, but it doesn’t introduce a functional correctness defect in the auth decision itself (DB fallback still happens).

adjudication_records.issue_text: getCachedIdentityPermissions returns cache.ErrNotFound for TypeRenderService on every request, forcing a full DB fetch every time; this regresses caching for render-service identity types (or the new switch is misleading dead code)

adjudication.rationale: In the new `getCachedIdentityPermissions` switch, `types.TypeRenderService` unconditionally returns `cache.ErrNotFound` (no cache lookup). Since `Service.Check` and `Service.List` now consult `getCachedIdentityPermissions` first and only then fall back to `getIdentityPermissions`, render-service requests will always take the fallback path. Additionally, this diff removed the prior cache-hit logic inside `getUserPermissions` / `getAnonymousPermissions`, so if render-service identities previously benefited from those caches via `getIdentityPermissions`, that caching would no longer apply. This is a concrete diff-grounded performance/behavior change, though it’s not provably a correctness bug without seeing how `getIdentityPermissions` handles `TypeRenderService`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The cached permission map (map[string]bool) is returned by reference from the shared cache and used across concurrent requests; if any consumer mutates it, the cache is corrupted for all readers—it should be treated as immutable or copied

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows cached permission maps are returned directly from the cache without copying (e.g., getCachedIdentityPermissions returns the `map[string]bool` obtained via `s.permCache.Get(...)` in multiple branches). Since Go maps are reference types, this exposes the shared cached map instance to callers (e.g., Check/List -> checkPermission/listPermission). The diff doesn’t prove any downstream code mutates the map, so a concrete corruption bug isn’t verifiable from the diff alone, but the finding is a specific, diff-grounded risk: consumers must treat the returned map as immutable or the cache layer should defensively copy.

adjudication_records.issue_text: On denial-cache hit, requestCount is incremented with "false", "true" labels identical to the DB path, making cache-hit denies indistinguishable from DB denies in metrics

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new denial-cache short-circuit path increments `requestCount` with `WithLabelValues("false", "true", ...)` (see the `permDenialCache.Get` hit branch). The non-cache (DB/fallback) deny path also increments `requestCount` with the same `WithLabelValues("false", "true", ...)` just before returning. So, as the finding states, cache-hit denies are not distinguishable from DB-path denies via `requestCount` labels based on what’s shown in the diff. This is an observability/metrics design issue rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test covers invalidation of permDenialCache when permissions change (e.g., a previously-denied resource must be allowed after a write/batch-set that clears permCache)

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new negative cache `permDenialCache` in `Service.Check`: it short-circuits to `Allowed: false` if a denial key is present, and it sets that key whenever a DB-backed check returns `!allowed` (service.go: new `permDenialCache` field, early-return block, and `Set` on denial). The new tests cover allow-from-permCache, DB fallback, and explicit denial entry, but none exercise what happens when permissions later change to allowed while a denial entry remains (i.e., there is no test asserting invalidation/clearing/override behavior for `permDenialCache`). Also, the diff shows no explicit invalidation of `permDenialCache` anywhere, only TTL-based expiry, so the edge-case is both untested and potentially significant.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The removed test 'should return permissions from cache if available' is only partially replaced; no test asserts that getUserPermissions still populates the cache after a DB fetch, so a regression where the cache is never written would go unnoticed

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the `getUserPermissions` test case that asserted a cache hit path, and the new tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) only validate reading from `permCache`/`permDenialCache` and fallback-to-DB behavior in `Check`/`List`. Nothing in the added tests asserts that after a DB-backed permission fetch (`getIdentityPermissions` → `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`), the service writes results into `s.permCache` for future requests. Whether the cache write exists or not isn’t shown in this diff chunk, but the finding correctly identifies a specific missing regression test for cache population after a miss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: When cached permissions are used for List, results may be stale with no versioning; List on a cache hit never validates against the DB even when permCache was populated long ago relative to idCache (different TTLs), which can list stale resources

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.List`, the new logic first calls `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` and, on a cache hit (`err == nil`), proceeds to `s.listPermission(...)` without calling `getIdentityPermissions(...)` (DB-backed) at all (see `func (s *Service) List`: the `if err == nil { ... } else { ... getIdentityPermissions ... }` split). Since `permCache` entries are plain `map[string]bool` with only TTL-based expiry and no versioning/invalidation tied to permission changes, a cache hit can return stale permissions and thus stale `List` results until expiry. This is a concrete behavior implied by the diff; it’s more of a cache-consistency/authorization-staleness concern than a definite functional bug given TTL-based caching may be intended.
